newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban official says US refuses recognition.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban official says US refuses recognition.

text.p: A leader of Afghanistan's Taleban militia said on Wednesday that a U.S. official had told him Washington would not recognise the Taleban administration.
Mullah Wakil Ahmed, a top aide of Taleban leader Mullah Mohammed Omar, said he had met U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robin Raphel for 90 minutes in Islamabad on Tuesday.
A U.S. Embassy spokesman confirmed the meeting, one of the highest-level contacts to date between Washington and the purist Islamic movement now ruling most of Afghanistan.
The spokesman gave no details of their talks, but Ahmed said they had focused on the Taleban's quest for international recognition and American concern about the narcotics trade.
"We asked for official recognition of our government and the Americans for their part voiced their apprehensions about opium poppy cultivation," Ahmed told Reuters by telephone.

"We told Raphel that being Moslems we are also concerned about narcotics, but we have some problems. We cannot do it single-handedly. The people of Afghanistan are confronted with numerous economic problems and have no other options," he said.
Afghanistan, impoverished by 18 years of conflict, is one of the world's top producers of opium, from which heroin is made.
"We told Raphel it would be better to deal with us on a government-to-government basis and realise the realities on the ground," Ahmed said.
The Taleban captured Kabul on September 27, but no country has yet formally recognised their interim administration.
Ahmed quoted Raphel as saying the United States could not recognise the Taleban administration and would only recognise a broad-based government in which all factions were represented.
"We said we are ready to negotiate, but the opposition are not willing. They comprise different groups and they don't speak with one voice," the Taleban leader said.
The Taleban, seeking to impose their strict version of Islam across Afghanistan, are battling forces led by General Abdul Rashid Dostum and Ahmad Shah Masood north of Kabul.
Ahmed said he was planning to lead a four-member Taleban delegation that would leave for the United States on Thursday.

The delegation includes the Taleban's nominee for permanent representative at the United Nations, Maulvi Abdul Hakim Mujahid, the militia's acting Minister for Refugee, Affairs Abdul Rakib, and an Islamabad-based Afghan diplomat, Abdul Wahhab.
Ahmed said the delegation would meet State Department officials in Washington and then go to New York to claim Afghanistan's seat at the United Nations.
The ousted Afghan government led by President Burhanuddin Rabbani also claims the seat, but the United Nations has deferred a decision on who should occupy it.
The United States has denied accusations made by the Iranian media and by anti-Taleban factions that it supports the Islamic militia, saying it favours no Afghan group over another.
Raphel told a news conference in Islamabad that the United States had no plans "in the foreseeable future" to reopen its embassy in Kabul, closed since 1989.
"The security situation is not such that we would be able to reopen," she said, citing a recent opposition air strike that destroyed a section of the embassy's perimeter wall.
Raphel said the United States continued to "place our whole faith and trust" in U.N. efforts to broker a peace settlement in Afghanistan, despite their apparent lack of progress.
She made no mention of her meeting with Ahmed, which took place during a two-day visit to Pakistan ahead of a regional meeting of U.S. ambassadors in the Bangladeshi capital Dhaka.
